summary: Describes an SMIv2 MIB for devices that implement the Differentiated Services architecture, for monitoring and configuration. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: DiffServ is the set of rules that let a network treat important traffic differently from ordinary traffic, by marking packets, measuring them, and queueing them in a particular way. This RFC describes how a manager inspects and changes all of that on a router using SNMP. The MIB models the work as a chain of steps, where each step says what happens next.

questions: how to configure diffserv with snmp
what is a rowpointer in snmp
subtitle: An SNMP MIB that lets managers monitor and configure how a router classifies, meters, marks, drops, queues and schedules packets.

tldr.problem: Differentiated Services lets a network give different treatment to different kinds of traffic, but the architecture says nothing about how a router should be built, so there was no common way to configure or inspect what a router is actually doing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an SMIv2 MIB module that models the processing path as a chain of pointers: each classifier, meter, action, dropper, queue and scheduler points at the next one, and separate tables hold the parameters such as token bucket rates.
tldr.outcome: A management system can read and write a router's DiffServ policy through SNMP, and because the pointers can point at entries in other MIB modules, new ciphers, filters and scheduling methods can be added without changing this document.

today:
RFC 3289 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the SNMP MIB for the Differentiated Services Architecture.

The document recommends SNMPv3 with the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model for any use of it, and notes that the MIB was written so that other MIB modules can add new filters, meters and scheduling methods without changing it.

sections.title: The SNMP Management Framework
sections.content:
The SNMP Management Framework presently consists of five major components. There is an overall architecture, described in RFC 2571. There are mechanisms for describing and naming objects and events for the purpose of management: the first version of the Structure of Management Information is called SMIv1 and is described in RFC 1155, RFC 1212 and RFC 1215, and the second version, SMIv2, is described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. There are message protocols for transferring management information: SNMPv1 in RFC 1157, SNMPv2c in RFC 1901 and RFC 1906, and SNMPv3 in RFC 1906, RFC 2572 and RFC 2574. There are protocol operations for accessing management information, the first set in RFC 1157 and a second set in RFC 1905. And there is a set of fundamental applications described in RFC 2573 and the view-based access control mechanism described in RFC 2575.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base, and objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms defined in the SMI. This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to SMIv2. A MIB conforming to SMIv1 can be produced through the appropriate translations, and the resulting translated MIB must be semantically equivalent, except where objects or events are omitted because no translation is possible, the use of Counter64 being the example. Some machine-readable information in SMIv2 is converted into textual descriptions in SMIv1 during the translation, and that loss of machine-readable information is not considered to change the semantics of the MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is how a manager asks a device about itself and tells it to change. The MIB is the catalogue of things a manager can ask about. This RFC adds a new catalogue for the DiffServ part of a router.

sections.title: MIB Overview
sections.content:
The Differentiated Services Architecture does not specify how an implementation should be assembled. The informal management model for a DiffServ router describes a general approach to implementation design or to user interface design, but its components could be assembled in a different way. Traffic conforming to a meter might be run through a second meter, or reclassified.

This MIB models the same functional data path elements, allowing the network manager to assemble them in any fashion that meets the relevant policy. Those elements are classifiers, meters, actions of various sorts, queues and schedulers.

In many of the tables a distinction is drawn between the structure of the policy, which is do this then do that, and the parameters applied to specific policy elements. The concept is that a set of parameters, such as the values that describe a specific token bucket, might be configured once and applied to many interfaces.

The RowPointer textual convention is therefore used in two ways in this MIB. It is defined for the purpose of connecting an object to an entry dynamically: the RowPointer object identifies the first object in the target entry, and in so doing points to the entire entry. It is used as a connector between successive functional data path elements, and as the link between the policy structure and the parameters that are used. When used as a connector it says what happens next, and when used to indicate parameters it says specifically what is meant.

The use of RowPointers as connectors allows for the simple extension of the MIB. The pointers, whether next or specific, may point to entries defined in other MIB modules. The only type of meter defined in this MIB is a token bucket meter; if another type of meter is required, another MIB could describe that type, and the meter's specific pointer could point to it. Similarly, if a new action is required, the next pointer of the previous functional data path element could point to an entry defined in another MIB, public or proprietary.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is in two halves. One half says the order of operations: classify, then meter, then act, then queue. The other half holds the numbers: the rate of a token bucket, the threshold of a queue. Each half is a table, and one points at the other.

sections.title: The Processing Path
sections.content:
An interface has an ingress and an egress direction, and will generally have a different policy in each direction. As traffic enters an edge interface it may be classified, metered, counted and marked. Traffic leaving the same interface might be remarked according to the contract with the next network, queued to manage the bandwidth, and so on. The functional data path elements used on ingress and on egress are of the same type, but may be structured in very different ways to implement the relevant policies.

The first step in applying a policy is therefore determining what policy applies. The MIB does that with a table of pointers to the first functional data path element, indexed by interface and by direction on that interface. The content of each entry is a single RowPointer, which points to that functional data path element. When the start pointer in a direction on an interface is undefined or is set to zeroDotZero, the implication is that there is no specific policy to apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Each interface has two directions, and the rules are usually different for each. The MIB starts with one small table that says, for every interface and direction, where the processing begins.

sections.title: Classifiers
sections.content:
Classifiers are used to differentiate among types of traffic. In the Differentiated Services architecture one usually discusses a behaviour aggregate identified by the application of one or more Differentiated Services Code Points. However, especially at network edges, which include hosts and first hop routers serving hosts, traffic may arrive unmarked or the marks may not be trusted. In these cases one applies a multi-field classifier, which may select an aggregate as coarse as all traffic, as fine as a specific microflow identified by IP addresses, IP protocol and TCP or UDP ports, or a variety of slices in between.

Classifiers can be simple or complex. In a core interface one would expect to find simple behaviour aggregate classification. At an edge interface one might first ask what application is being used, meter the arriving traffic, and then apply different policies to the non-conforming traffic depending on the Autonomous System number advertising the destination address. To do that, traffic must be classified, metered and then reclassified. The MIB therefore defines separate classifiers, which may be applied at any point in processing and may have different content as needed.

The MIB also allows for ambiguous classification in a structured fashion. Traffic classification must in the end be unambiguous, so it must be known for certain what policy applies to any given packet. Writing an unambiguous specification is often tedious, while writing a specification in steps that permit and exclude various kinds of traffic may be simpler and more intuitive. In such a case the classification steps are enumerated, all classification elements of one precedence are applied as if in parallel, and then all the elements of the next precedence.

A classifier consists of classifier elements, and a classifier element identifies a specific set of traffic that forms part of a behaviour aggregate. Other classifier elements within the same classifier may identify other traffic that also falls into that aggregate. To identify AF traffic for the aggregate AF1, for example, one might implement separate classifier elements for AF11, AF12 and AF13 within the same classifier, pointing to the same subsequent meter.

A classifier element is a structural element indexed by classifier ID and element ID. It has a precedence value, allowing for the structured ambiguity described above, a specific pointer that identifies what rule is to be applied, and a next pointer directing traffic matching the classifier to the next functional data path element. If the next pointer is zeroDotZero there is no further differentiated services processing for that behaviour aggregate, but if the specific pointer is zeroDotZero the device is misconfigured, and the classifier element should be operationally treated as if it were not present.

The MIB defines a single classifier parameter entry, the multi-field classifier, and as a parameter a filter may be specified once and applied to many interfaces. That filter matches an IP source address prefix, including a host, a CIDR prefix or any source address; an IP destination address prefix on the same terms; an IPv6 Flow ID; an IP protocol or any; a TCP, UDP or SCTP source port range, including any; a TCP, UDP or SCTP destination port range, including any; and a Differentiated Services Code Point. The behaviour aggregate filter is a special case of this filter in which only the DSCP is specified.
sections.plainLanguage: Classification is how the router decides which traffic a rule applies to. The MIB offers one general-purpose filter that can look at the addresses, the ports, the protocol and the DSCP, and you can leave any of them out. Several filter elements can be combined, and they are tried in order of precedence, so a policy can be written as a series of steps rather than one long condition.

sections.title: Meters and Actions
sections.content:
A meter and a shaper are functions that operate on opposing ends of a link. A shaper schedules traffic for transmission at specific times in order to approximate a particular line speed. A meter integrates the arrival rate of traffic and determines whether the shaper at the far end was correctly applied, or whether the behaviour of the application is naturally close enough to such behaviour to be acceptable under a given policy.

A common type of meter is the token bucket meter. This type assumes the use of a shaper at a previous node, and it specifies the acceptable arrival rate and quantifies the acceptable variability, often by specifying a burst size or an interval. Since rate equals quantity over time, specifying any two of those parameters implies the third, and a large interval provides for a forgiving system. Multiple rates may be specified, as in AF, such that a subset of the traffic, up to one rate, is accepted with one set of guarantees, and traffic in excess of that but below another rate has a different set of guarantees.

The Meter Table is a structural table specifying a specific functional data path element, and its entry consists essentially of three RowPointers: a succeed pointer for traffic conforming to the meter, a fail pointer for traffic not conforming to the meter, and a specific pointer identifying the parameters in question. The document is candid that this structure is a bow to SNMP's limitations, and that it would be better to have a structure with N rates and N+1 next pointers with a single algorithm specified. In this MIB, multiple meter entries connected by the fail link are understood to contain the parameters for a specified algorithm, and traffic conforming to a given rate follows their succeed paths. Only token bucket parameters are specified here.

The Token Bucket Parameters Table defines a token bucket meter, and as a parameter a token bucket may be specified once and applied to many interfaces. If a token bucket has N rates it has N+1 potential outcomes: the stream is slower than and therefore conforms to all the rates, it fails the first few but is slower than and therefore conforms to the higher rates, or it fails all of them. Multi-rate meters should therefore specify their rates in monotonically increasing order, passing through the meter fail pointer from more committed to more excess rates, and finally falling through to the set of actions that apply to traffic conforming to none of the specified rates. At each rate the rate is derivable from the burst size and the interval.

Actions are the things a differentiated services interface may do to a packet in transit. At a minimum such a policy might calculate statistics on traffic in various configured classes, mark it with a DSCP, drop it, or enqueue it before passing it on. Actions are composed of a structural element, the Action Table, and various component action entries that may be applied.

The Action Table identifies sequences of actions to be applied to a packet, with successive actions chained through the next pointer, ultimately resulting in zeroDotZero, indicating that the policy is complete, a pointer to a queue, or a pointer to some other functional data path element. The count action accumulates statistics pertaining to traffic passing through a given path through the policy, and is intended to be useful for usage-based billing, for statistical studies, or for analysis of the behaviour of a policy in a given network; its counters show the number of packets and bytes encountered on the path since the discontinuity time. The designers expect every path through a policy to have a corresponding counter, but in the current design that is left to the network manager's option, so the assurance of proper debugging and accounting is left with the policy designer.

The Mark Action table is unusual: it might be viewed not so much as an array of single-object entries as an array of OBJECT-IDENTIFIER conventions, because the object identifier of a mark action instance conveys all the necessary information, namely that packets are to be marked with the requisite DSCP. The index for that table is therefore read-only, and is both the entry's index and its only value.

The Algorithmic Drop Table identifies a dropping algorithm, drops packets and counts the drops. When the algorithm is always drop this is simple; when it calls for head-drop, tail-drop or a variety of Active Queue Management the queue is inspected, and for Active Queue Management additional parameters are required. What may not be clear from the name is that an Algorithmic Drop action often does not drop traffic, since algorithms other than always drop normally drop a few percent of packets at most. The Random Drop Table is an extension of it for queues whose depth is actively managed, and its parameters include the target case mean queue depth, the worst case mean queue depth, the maximum drop rate expressed as drops per thousand, the coefficient of an exponentially weighted moving average expressed as the numerator of a fraction whose denominator is 65536, and the sampling rate. In the MIB module the minimum and maximum threshold objects represent Qmin and Qmax, the algorithmic drop threshold object represents Qclip, and the inverse probability object represents the maximum drop probability.
sections.plainLanguage: The meter is the part that watches the arrival rate and decides whether the traffic is inside the contract. The MIB represents it with two pointers: one for traffic that fits, one for traffic that does not, and the excess traffic can be chained into another meter for the next rate down. The actions are what then happen: count it, mark it, drop it or put it in a queue.

sections.title: Queues and Schedulers
sections.content:
Queues and schedulers are inter-related in their use of queuing techniques, and by combining them it is possible to build multi-level schedulers, such as those which treat a set of queues as having priority among them and, at a specific priority, find a secondary weighted fair queuing scheduler with some number of queues.

The Queue Table models simple FIFO queues, and the Scheduler Table allows flexibility in constructing both simple and more complex queuing hierarchies from those queues. Queue table entries are pointed at by the next attributes of upstream elements, and multiple upstream elements may direct their traffic to the same queue entry. The Assured Forwarding per-hop behaviour, for example, suggests that all traffic marked AF11, AF12 or AF13 be placed in the same queue after metering without reordering, which is done by having the upstream algorithmic drop pointers each point to the same queue entry.

A common requirement of a queue is that its traffic enjoy a certain minimum or maximum rate, or that it be given a certain priority. Functionally the selection of such a thing is a function of a scheduler, but the parameter is associated with the queue, using the Minimum or Maximum Rate Parameters Table.

The scheduler, and therefore the Scheduler Table, accepts inputs from either queues or a preceding scheduler. When the output rate of a queue or scheduler must be given a minimum rate or a priority, the Minimum Rate Table is used. Rates may be expressed as absolute rates or as a fraction of the interface speed, and imply the use of a rate-based scheduler such as weighted fair queuing or weighted round robin. The use of a priority implies the use of a priority scheduler. Only one of the absolute or relative rates needs to be set; the other takes the relevant value as a result. Excess capacity is distributed proportionally among the inputs to a scheduler using the assured rate.

When a priority scheduler is used, its effect is to give the queue the entire capacity of the subject interface less the capacity used by higher priorities, if there is traffic present to use it. This is true regardless of the rate specifications applied to that queue or other queues on the interface, and policing excess traffic will mitigate this behaviour.

When the output rate of a queue or scheduler must be limited to at most a specified maximum rate, the Maximum Rate Table is used, with rates expressed as absolute rates or as a fraction of the interface speed. The definition of a multirate shaper requires multiple entries in that table: more than one rate is specified, and at any given time traffic is shaped to the lowest specified rate which exceeds the arrival rate of traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A queue holds packets and a scheduler decides whose turn it is to send. The MIB lets a queue be given a guaranteed share of the link, a priority, or a ceiling, and lets a scheduler take input from queues or from other schedulers, so a hierarchy of them can be built.

sections.title: Conventions and Extending the MIB
sections.content:
RowPointer is a textual convention used to identify a conceptual row in a MIB table by pointing to one of its objects. One of the ways this MIB uses it is to indicate succession, pointing to data path linkage table entries. For succession it answers the question what happens next. Rather than presume that the next table must be as specified in the conceptual model and providing its index, the RowPointer takes you to the MIB row representing that thing. In the Meter Table, for example, the fail pointer might take you to another meter, while the succeed pointer would take you to an action.

Because a RowPointer is not tied to any specific object except by the value it contains, it is possible and acceptable to use RowPointers to merge data paths. Traffic matching the DSCPs AF11, AF12 and AF13 might be presented to the same meter to perform the processing described in the Assured Forwarding per-hop behaviour. Another use would be to merge data paths from several interfaces, so that they share a common set of counters and a common policy. The document notes that such configurations may have related implementation issues, since if the processing for the interfaces is implemented in multiple forwarding engines the engines will need to communicate, and that an implementation which fails to provide this capability is not considered to have failed the intention of the MIB.

It is possible that a path through a device following a set of RowPointers is indeterminate, ending in a dangling RowPointer. For both zeroDotZero and a dangling pointer it is assumed that the data path ends and the traffic should be given to the next logical part of the device, usually a forwarding process or a transmission engine.

RowPointer is also used to indicate parameterization. For indirection, the idea is to allow other MIBs, including proprietary ones, to define new and arcane filters, such as MAC headers, IPv4 and IPv6 headers and BGP Communities, while still using the structures of this MIB. The document describes this as a form of class inheritance: it allows base object definitions to be extended in proprietary or standard ways by other documents. RowPointer also clearly indicates that the identified conceptual row's content does not change, so they can be pointed to by more than one data path linkage table entry at the same time.

A number of conceptual tables use as an index an arbitrary integer value, unique across the scope of the agent. To help with multi-manager row-creation problems, each such table has an associated NextFree variable, for example diffServClfrNextFree, which provides a suitable value for the index of the next row to be created, and the value zero is used to indicate that the agent can configure no more entries. The table also has a columnar Status attribute with RowStatus syntax. If a manager attempts to create a row, the agent will create it and return success, or return an error if it has insufficient resources or such a row already exists, and the manager must be prepared to try again, probably by re-reading the NextFree value in case a second manager got in between.

To simplify creation and deletion of rows, the agent is expected to assist in maintaining consistency, perhaps by maintaining internal usage counters for any row that might be pointed to by a RowPointer. When a RowPointer is created or written and the row it points to does not exist, the SET returns an inconsistentValue error. When a RowStatus variable is set to destroy but the usage counter is non-zero, the SET returns no error but the indicated row is left intact, and the agent should remove it later if the counter reaches zero.

With the structures of this MIB divided into data path linkage tables and parameterization tables, and with the use of RowPointer, new linkage and parameterization tables can be defined in other MIB modules and used with the tables defined here. The MIB does not limit the type of entries its RowPointer attributes can point to, so new functional data path elements can be defined in other MIBs and integrated with the ones here. It is more likely that new parameterization tables will be created in other MIBs as new methods get deployed, for example different kinds of filters, new scheduling methods and new scheduling parameter tables. Both new linkage tables and new parameterization tables can be added without changing this document or affecting the existing tables and their usage.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the chain is held together by pointers rather than by fixed table names, a future MIB can add a new kind of filter, meter or scheduler and simply point at it. The document also explains how a manager creates rows without colliding with another manager, and how the device keeps itself consistent when rows are pointed at from more than one place.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
It is clear that this MIB is potentially useful for configuration, and that anything that can be configured can be misconfigured, with potentially disastrous effects. At the time of writing, no security holes have been identified beyond those that SNMP security is itself intended to address. These relate primarily to controlled access to sensitive information and the ability to configure a device, or which might result from operator error, which is beyond the scope of any security architecture.

There are many read-write and read-create management objects defined in this MIB, and such objects are often sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. The support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations, and the use of SNMP Version 3 is recommended over prior versions for configuration control, as its security model is improved.

There are a number of managed objects in this MIB that may contain information that is sensitive from a business perspective, in that they may represent a customer's service contract or the filters that the service provider chooses to apply to a customer's ingress or egress traffic. There are no objects which are sensitive in their own right, such as passwords or monetary amounts. It may be important to control even GET access to these objects, and possibly to encrypt the values of these objects when sending them over the network via SNMP.

SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment, and even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is still no control over who on that network is allowed to access the objects in this MIB. It is recommended that implementors consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, and specifically the use of the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model. It is then a customer or user responsibility to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to an instance of this MIB is properly configured to give access only to those principals that have legitimate rights to read or change the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: This MIB can change how a router treats your traffic, so it needs the same care as any other configuration surface. The document's advice is to use SNMPv3 with its access control, and to remember that some of the values it exposes reveal a customer's contract or the filters applied to their traffic.

root.label: Data Path
root.note: One per interface and direction, named by the Data Path Table

children.label: Meter
children.note: Checks the arrival rate, with a succeed and a fail path

children.label: Algorithmic Drop
children.note: Applies a drop algorithm to a queue

children.label: Scheduler
children.note: Decides whose turn it is to send

viz.caption: THE TWO KINDS OF TABLE IN THE MIB (RFC 3289)

cells: The structure of the policy: do this, then do that
The values applied to a policy element, such as the rates of a token bucket
By RowPointers that say what happens next
By a RowPointer that says specifically what is meant
Structural elements may be shared, but then the counters are shared too
The same parameters may be applied to many interfaces

items.title: Source address prefix
items.text: A host, a CIDR prefix, or any source address.

items.title: Destination address prefix
items.text: A host, a CIDR prefix, or any destination address.

items.title: Source port range
items.text: TCP, UDP or SCTP, or any.

items.title: Destination port range
items.text: TCP, UDP or SCTP, or any.

items.title: DSCP
items.text: The code point; a behaviour aggregate filter is this filter with only the DSCP set.

items.title: Count
items.text: Accumulates statistics on the traffic passing through a path, for billing or for analysis.

items.title: DSCP mark
items.text: Marks the packet with a code point; the table index is the code point itself.

items.title: Algorithmic drop
items.text: Applies a drop algorithm to a queue, usually active queue management, and counts the drops.

items.title: Random drop
items.text: Parameters for a random dropper: queue thresholds, drop probability, moving-average weight and sampling rate.
